title: The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg
text:
Hadleyburg was famous for being the most honest and incorruptible town in the region. Its children were taught honesty from the cradle and kept far from temptation. One day the town offended a passing stranger, and he decided to take revenge on the whole place.

Years later he returned and left a heavy sack at the house of an old bank cashier, Edward Richards, with a note. It said the sack held gold worth about forty thousand dollars, meant as a reward for a Hadleyburg man who had once given the stranger twenty dollars and a piece of good advice. The man who could repeat the remark would get the gold.

Then the stranger sent letters to nineteen of the town's leading citizens. Each one was told privately the exact remark and was invited to claim the prize. None of them had given the money, but each of them sent in a claim.

At a great town meeting, the claims were opened one by one, and the leading citizens were exposed, in front of everyone, as liars and cheats. Richards was spared only because the man reading the claims quietly held his back. The sack turned out to hold gilded lead. Disgraced, the town changed its name and its motto.
lesson: A group that has never tested its virtue may find out all at once that it lacks it. Honesty that depends on never meeting temptation is not yet honesty.
people: Edward and Mary Richards, the nineteen leading citizens of Hadleyburg, the stranger
source: Mark Twain, The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg (1899)
